references.text: Moses had just received the two tablets of the testimony, written on both sides by God's own hand, before he threw them down.
Moses recounts the event where he saw Israel's sin with the golden calf and cast the tablets from his hands and broke them.
Describes how the golden calf was made and the people danced around it, which is what Moses saw as he approached the camp.
God commands Moses to carve out new stone tablets in place of the first ones that he had broken.
Moses is told to carve out new tablets after the first ones were shattered at the foot of the mountain.
Dance (מְחֹלֹת) is also mentioned when Miriam and the women danced before the Lord, in contrast to the sinful dancing around the golden calf.
Stephen refers to this event in his speech, where the Israelites made a calf and rejoiced over the work of their hands.
Both texts unfold the dynamic between the Lord's burning anger and Moses' emotional response as mediator for a sinful people.
Direct narrative connection: The breaking of the first tablets (32:19) leads directly to the carving of new tablets (34:4).
Moses' own recounting and theological interpretation of the event in Deuteronomy confirms and illuminates the action in Exodus.
A thematic parallel showing the consequences of covenant breaking: destruction of covenant symbols (Exodus) leads to surrender to enemies (Judges).
